Does not understand English, but bases his judgment on the sound of the voice.

‘Alberto Montani, a confectioner, states that he was among the first people to go upstairs. He heard the voices being discussed. The rough voice belonged to a Frenchman. He could pick out several words, and the speaker seemed to be arguing against something. He could not understand the words spoken by the high-pitched voice. It spoke rapidly, with an uneven rhythm. He believes it was a Russian voice. He confirms the other witnesses’ general account. He is Italian and has never spoken with anyone from Russia.

‘Several witnesses were called back and stated that the chimneys in every room on the fourth floor were too narrow for a person to pass through. The word “sweeps” referred to round chimney brushes of the kind used by chimney cleaners. These brushes had been pushed up and down every chimney passage in the house. There was no rear passage by which anyone could have come down while the group was going upstairs. Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body was jammed into the chimney so tightly that four or five people had to pull together to bring it down.

‘Paul Dumas, a doctor, states that he was summoned to examine the bodies around dawn. Both were then lying on the coarse fabric supporting the bed in the room where Mademoiselle L. had been found. The young woman’s body was badly bruised and scraped. Being forced up the chimney would adequately explain these injuries. Her throat was severely grazed. There were several deep scratches just below her chin, along with a row of dark marks that were clearly impressions left by fingers. Her face was horribly discoloured, and her eyes bulged. She had bitten partway through her tongue. A large bruise was found at the top of her stomach, apparently caused by the pressure of a knee. In M. Dumas’s opinion, Mademoiselle L’Espanaye had been strangled by an unknown person or persons. Her mother’s body was horribly mutilated. Every bone in her right arm and leg was broken to some degree. The left shinbone and all the ribs on the left side were badly splintered. The entire body was severely bruised and discoloured. It was impossible to determine how these injuries had been caused. A heavy wooden club, a broad iron bar, a chair—any large, heavy, blunt weapon—could have done such damage in the hands of a very strong man. No woman could have delivered those blows, whatever weapon she used. When the witness saw the dead woman’s head, it was completely detached from her body and badly shattered as well. Her throat had clearly been cut with a very sharp tool, probably a razor.’

Raymond felt the powerful excitement of returning health. As general of the Athenians, he believed he held a position worthy of his ambition. He hoped to conquer Constantinople, and saw that future victory as a landmark amid the empty stretch of centuries, a feat unmatched in human history. The city, with its great historical associations and a setting whose beauty amazed the world, had been a Muslim stronghold for hundreds of years. Now it would be freed from slavery and barbarism and restored to a people celebrated for their genius, civilization, and love of liberty. Perdita settled into his renewed companionship, his love, his hopes, and his fame as a lover of comfort might settle onto a luxurious couch. Every thought brought delight; every feeling seemed to bathe in a warm, soothing atmosphere perfectly suited to it.

We reached Kishan on July 7. Throughout our journey, the weather had been calm. Each morning we left our camp before dawn and watched the shadows withdraw from the hills and valleys as the approaching sun filled the sky with gold. With the lively spirit of their country, the soldiers accompanying us responded to nature’s beauty with enthusiastic delight. They greeted the sunrise with triumphant music, and snatches of birdsong filled the pauses between the notes. At midday we put up our tents in a shaded valley or beneath the trees in a mountain wood. The murmur of a stream running over pebbles helped us drift into welcome sleep. Our evening march was calmer and even more delightful than the morning’s restless excitement. When the band played, its musicians instinctively chose tunes of gentler feeling. A lover’s farewell or a lament for someone absent would lead into a solemn hymn that closed the music. It matched the evening’s peaceful beauty and lifted our minds toward grand, religious thoughts. Often everyone fell silent so that we could hear the nightingale, while fireflies danced in bright patterns and the aziolo’s soft calls promised us fair weather. In the valleys we were surrounded by gentle shadows and rocks touched with beautiful colours. From the mountains, Greece lay beneath us like a living map: its famous peaks pierced the sky, and its rivers traced silver lines through the fertile country. We English travellers gazed with delight at this magnificent scene, scarcely daring to breathe. It was so different from the quiet colours and melancholy beauty of our own countryside. After we left Macedonia, the fertile but low-lying plains of Thrace offered fewer beautiful views. Yet the journey remained interesting. An advance guard announced our arrival, and the country people quickly set about preparing to honour Lord Raymond.

But I must warn you now that I shall tell Sybil everything. She’s having lunch with me tomorrow to talk about bonnets, and if Mr. Podgers discovers that you have a bad temper, or are likely to get gout, or have a wife living in Bayswater, I shall certainly give her all the details.’

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. ‘I’m not afraid,’ he replied. ‘Sybil knows me as well as I know her.’

‘Ah! I’m rather sorry to hear that. Marriage ought to be based on a mutual misunderstanding. No, I’m not cynical at all. I simply have experience, though that amounts to much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is desperate to have his palm read. Don’t tell him he’s engaged to one of London’s most beautiful girls. The Morning Post reported that a month ago.’

‘Dear Lady Windermere,’ exclaimed the Marchioness of Jedburgh, ‘please let Mr. Podgers stay here a little longer. He has just told me I ought to go on the stage, and I find it so interesting.’

‘If he told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I shall certainly take him away. Come here immediately, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.’

‘Well,’ said Lady Jedburgh, pouting a little as she got up from the sofa, ‘if I’m not allowed to go on the stage, I must at least be allowed to join the audience.’

‘Naturally. We shall all be in the audience,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘Now, Mr. Podgers, make sure you tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is a particular favourite of mine.’

But the moment Mr. Podgers looked at Lord Arthur’s hand, he turned strangely pale and fell silent. He seemed to shudder, and his thick, bushy eyebrows jerked in the peculiar, irritating way they did when something confused him. Then large drops of sweat appeared on his yellow forehead like poisonous dew, while his plump fingers became cold and damp.

Lord Arthur noticed these unusual signs of distress. For the first time in his life, he too felt afraid. His first urge was to rush out of the room, but he held himself back. Whatever the worst might be, knowing it would be better than remaining in this dreadful uncertainty.

‘I’m waiting, Mr. Podgers,’ he said.

‘We’re all waiting,’ Lady Windermere added in her brisk, impatient way. But the palm reader gave no answer.

‘I think Arthur must be going on the stage,’ said Lady Jedburgh, ‘and after the scolding you gave him, Mr. Podgers is afraid to say so.’
